item.title: Building and defending our digital territories: Reflections from an Ecofeminist perspectiveBy Silvina González Soler In a context marked by the rise of far-right movements, the concentration of technological power in...
item.description:
By Silvina González Soler

In a context marked by the rise of far-right movements, the concentration of technological power in the hands of a few companies, and a digital culture often characterized by surveillance, data extraction and the logic of constant performance, talking about digital resilience means asking ourselves a deeper question:

How do we want to move through increasingly hostile, violent and extractive digital spaces that are very much embedded in our lives, our movements and our communities?

A few months ago, at Women Deliver 2026, FRIDA facilitated a workshop on digital resilience and the construction of feminist digital territories alongside Jac sm Kee from Numun Fund. This workshop brought together people from different regions of the world, backgrounds and movements. From the outset, we didn’t want the session to be  a ‘training’ based on technical ‘solutions’, but a participatory space where we could collectively reflect on what it means to resist, look after one another and develop strategies within a digital ecosystem that is often not designed for our practices.

We began with a simple yet complex question:

What does digital resilience mean to us?

The choice of this concept was not trivial. We know that the word ‘resilience’ can be problematic: it is often used within a framework of constant individual adaptation, continuous improvement and the ability to withstand any adversity. A framework closely linked to the idea that we must always be able to do more, achieve more and endure more. From our feminist practices, we know that this cannot be the only answer.

However, we also recognized that the notion of resilience could open up a shared conversation amongst people with very diverse experiences. It allowed us to ask ourselves collectively what we do when digital spaces become hostile, when our communities face attacks, when platforms do not support our forms of organization, and when sustaining our movements involves navigating multiple risks.

The responses were varied and, in many ways, contradictory.

For some people, digital resilience appears to be an unavoidable necessity: we have no choice but to learn to resist and adapt, because feminist and social justice movements need to continue to exist and build within these spaces.

But at the same time, another dimension emerged very strongly: resilience can also be exhausting. It can become a constant demand placed on those who sustain communities, lead organisations and face the daily consequences of inhabiting digital spaces marked by violence, precariousness and a lack of control over the tools we use.

Building on this tension, we worked in groups to unpack the values we associate with digital resilience and how those values can be translated into concrete practices. We explored which strategies already exist within our organizations, what challenges we continue to face, and what new forms of collective ownership we can imagine.

Perhaps one of the most important lessons from the workshop was to remember that digital resilience cannot be thought of solely in terms of improvement or the search for solutions. We also need to acknowledge the exhaustion, frustration and anger that so often accompany our digital experiences.

There is something deeply political in being able to say: this exhausts us, this hurts us, this enrages us.

From a feminist perspective, these feelings of unease are not individual failings that we need to correct. They are signs that can help us identify what we need to transform. Feminist anger, discomfort and weariness can also be creative drivers for imagining other forms of organization and other possible futures.

Because we are not navigating these digital spaces alone.

Thinking about digital resilience from a feminist perspective involves reclaiming the collective dimension of care, creation and defence. It involves remembering that technology is not neutral: today’s digital spaces were built according to specific priorities, often guided by commercial interests and business models that do not necessarily meet our needs.

But that is not the only possibility. From Ecofeminist perspectives, we understand that our bodies inhabit multiple territories that we need to care for and defend. The digital territory is also part of this fabric: it is a space where we build connections, share knowledge, organize resistance and create possible worlds.

Our digital body-territory deserves to be cared for with tenderness and respect. It deserves to be a space where we can reclaim agency and where we can imagine other ways of relating to technology.

Building feminist digital territories does not simply mean learning to protect ourselves from existing threats. It also means challenging the way we want to be present there. It means creating digital spaces where care, solidarity, accessibility and justice are central principles.

Digital resilience, then, does not have to be the ability to endure a system that constantly excludes us. It can become a collective practice to transform that system and build, together, digital territories where our communities can exist, create and thrive.

item.title: Looking to young feminist leaders past, present and futureThis past April FRIDA travelled to Oxford, England and Narrm, Australia for the 2026 Skoll World Forum and Women Deliver...
item.description:
This past April FRIDA travelled to Oxford, England and Narrm, Australia for the 2026 Skoll World Forum and Women Deliver 2026 respectively. Through broad yet intersecting themes that are incredibly important to both philanthropy and feminist movement building in this moment in history, it was important to us to centre, first and foremost, the political commitments and contributions of young feminist activists. 

As feminist and allied funds embark on the big, albeit not entirely new, questions that will guide how philanthropy shifts and reimagines itself in order to become the partner and ally that movements really need in this moment – we, inspired by the Australian Welcome to Country ritual – keep returning to the young feminists of FRIDA’s past, present and future. Young feminists who have not only posited these questions but have spent years developing the frameworks that may begin to answer them.

We turn to and foreground their expertise to illuminate the way.

The Skoll World Forum is a yearly event whose aim is to shine a spotlight on some of the most promising solutions and impactful social innovations and connect leaders who are driving social progress around the world. Funding through tension: catalyzing change in turbulent times, a side event at the World Forum, examined the possibilities for the philanthropic sector to adapt – in these times of polycrisis – to meaningfully support social justice efforts. 

“At a moment of compounding crises—including shrinking civic space, democratic backsliding, accelerating climate risk, and protracted armed conflict around the world—philanthropy is under increasing pressure to adapt. Yet while strategies are evolving, the underlying funding infrastructure and decision-making logic has not kept pace with the complexity and speed of the world we are operating in.” 

This side event convened leaders from global collaborative and intermediary funds to ask:

  • How do we balance trust in grantees with ever-increasing risks?  
  • Is now the time to be investing in systems or in the grassroots? Is it possible to think long-term when new urgent threats emerge so rapidly? 

Interested in reading more about FRIDA’s interventions at the Skoll World Forum? 

Click here

In this concurrent session, FRIDA and Numun Fund gathered with participants to envision a feminist tech resilient future, share alternatives, desires, core principles and ultimately an ownership that creates a safe and joyful digital territory. We chose to break away from tech systems that replicate systemic oppressions and power dynamics by imagining resilient practices and infrastructure.

Keep an eye out for the full publication on this warm, invigorating and inspiring session.

Hosted by The Adolescent Girls Investment Plan, this session fostered intergenerational accountability and collective action to uphold safeguarding as a shared commitment to protect and advance girls’ rights, agency and leadership in increasingly challenging environments.

Interested in FRIDA’S recommendations to fill safeguarding gaps?

Click here

Hosted By Urgent Action Fund for Feminist Activism, in this session, frontline activists and feminist funds made the case for resourcing collective care as an essential part of movement-building and sustenance, especially in times of acute crisis. 

Interested in how FRIDA resources collective Care?

Click here

Hosted by ILGA World, ILGA Oceania and Outright International, this session explored the lived realities of LGBTIQ+ individuals within feminist and SRHR movements, while interrogating the structural and political silos that continue to limit meaningful inclusion.

Interested in reading Paige, FRIDA CoED, experience of LBQ organizing in the Caribbean and finding acceptance and solidarity with the feminist movement?

Click here

item.title: Grantmaking for our future, now!The past few years have demanded so much of young feminist movement organisers. They have had to navigate unprecedented shifts...
item.description:
The past few years have demanded so much of young feminist movement organisers. They have had to navigate unprecedented shifts in the philanthropic ecosystem, a complex web of polycrises and shrinking philanthropic spending for key aspects of young feminist movement work. 

In the midst of these challenges and changes, FRIDA has continued to support young feminist activists through our reflexive grantmaking strategies. These grantmaking strategies are both responsive to the systemic challenges within philanthropy as a whole, as well as the hopes and dreams of the movements we support. 

Over the course of several years, FRIDA has revised, refined and co-created the ways it supports and accompanies grantee partners through their journey with and within the FRIDAverse. Our hope and mission is to continuously build a model that allows us to support and strengthen young feminist organizers in the ways most pertinent to them, including both financial and non-financial resources. Our practice situates each partner within a grant timeline, with different levels and kinds of support being offered throughout a grant cycle. FRIDA accompanies grantee partners intentionally, helping them to grow and thrive beyond their FRIDA grant, helping build sustainable, vibrant movement actors.

Through this growth and refinement in both our accompaniment strategies and grantmaking frameworks, in 2025 we were able to welcome 24 new grantee partners to the FRIDAverse! 

In the midst of shrinking resource pools and civic spaces within many global majority countries, we are excited to be able to keep supporting the movement actors who are often on the front lines of push back against oppressive regimes and harmful politics.

Our new partners are working on the front lines of some of the most confronting issues activists and communities face today. They are climate defenders, artists, community leaders and defiers of the odds in so many ways. Their optimism, innovation and hard work are an inspiration to their communities, the movements they serve and to us at FRIDA.

In the 2025 Cohort Zine you will find brief biographies of some of FRIDA’s new partners as well as information on the regions they are based in. Due to an increasingly hostile global political context, the amount we share about some of our partners and their work will vary depending on risk profile and regional contexts. We also share lovenotes, written by each of the new grantee partners, for their fellow grantee partners, the groups that voted for them and the wider FRIDAVerse. May their words of love and encouragement, as well as their work and courage, serve as inspiration to all of us.

FRIDA funds young feminist collectives and organizations who need not just financial resourcing, but a structured approach that meets them fully, where they are at. Due to shifts in the philanthropic ecosystem and shrinking philanthropic spending for key aspects of feminist movement building, our ability to do this work has grown more limited. If you believe in young feminist leadership and young feminist activism, please consider donating to FRIDA.

item.title: Meet FRIDA’s new Grantee Partner Cohort 🎊From growing conservatism and rapidly shrinking civil society space to the destruction of our shared ecosystem, the world as we’ve known it is...
item.description:
From growing conservatism and rapidly  shrinking civil society space to the  destruction of our shared ecosystem,  the world as we’ve known it is facing  challenges that can often feel insurmountable.  In the midst of these difficult realities,  young feminist organising provides a resilient and hopeful bright spot. Young feminist activists are part of a long history of youth activism and resistance, and we’re excited to be able to extend support to 25 new grantee partners in their individual and collective journeys to liberation. Their work stitches communities together, pushes back against human rights infringements, and helps to build the better world we all dream of.

In our last Call For Applications [CFA] in 2022, FRIDA received over 1000 applications and the process took 9 months and required a sizable budget and human capacity. Given current internal capacities and resources, in 2025 we decided to host a community-led CFA. We tapped into the FRIDAverse (Our incredible Grantee partners & advisors) to help bring new partners into our orbit and asked our community to recommend groups they knew were making an impact. At the end of the call, we emerged with 24 new grantee partners, each doing incredible, necessary work.

In this zine you will find brief biographies of some of FRIDA’s new partners as well as information on the regions they are based in. Due to an increasingly hostile global political context, the amount we share about some of our partners and their work will vary depending on risk profile and regional contexts. We will also share lovenotes, written by each of the new grantee partners, for their fellow grantee partners, the groups that voted for them and the wider FRIDAVerse. May their words of love and encouragement, as well as their work and courage, serve as inspiration to all of us.

item.title: This Giving Tuesday, Fund young feminist power.Across the world, young feminist organizers are defending bodily autonomy, resisting authoritarianism, protecting their territories and lands from exploitation, and...
item.description:
Across the world, young feminist organizers are defending bodily autonomy, resisting authoritarianism, protecting their territories and lands from exploitation, and fighting against a global rollback of human rights. They do this work with creativity and courage, grounded in lived experience and a clear understanding of the intersecting realities of race, gender, class, and disability. 

…and their work is urgent. 

Despite decades of trends and rhetoric around ‘localisation’, ‘equity’ and ‘movement building’, mainstream philanthropy continues to underfund the very actors and infrastructure necessary for change. These are young feminist organizations and groups that hold communities together after disasters, defend rights in the face of repression, and provide basic services where institutions have failed. Most young feminist groups operate with shoestring budgets and unpaid labour, whilst facing constant precarity created by short-term and project-bound funding that prioritizes funder objectives over what movements actually need to stay alive.

Youth-led groups – particularly those led by girls and gender-expansive youth – receive pennies in the funding ecosystem, not because they are ineffective, but because philanthropy is still biased towards scale, fluency in English, and solutions that are bureaucratically comfortable; ones that provide them with the metrics, impact indicators, and reports that extract the labour of grantee partners, but add  little true value to revolutionary and paradigm shifting grassroots organising. The majority of grants remain tied to projects and restrictions, signaling that philanthropy and institutions still put more trust in their own knowledge instead of the hard won expertise of their grantee and movement partners. 

Crisis after crisis, from armed conflict to climate disasters, we have seen how large institutions move slowly, and while youth-led groups tend to respond immediately to the urgent needs of their communities, they remain the most under-resourced. In today’s turbulent political climate marked by conflict, polarisation and backlash, these groups are asked to do more with even less. 

At FRIDA, we know that young feminist organisers have the knowledge and expertise to decide how to best respond to their needs. We know that young feminists are constantly adapting, experimenting, and innovating in the face of adversity. Everyday we see how young feminists are contributing to feminist discourse and challenging regressive patriarchal, white-centric and racist narratives. 15 years of witnessing and resourcing young feminist movements means that we know that flexible core funding works and that young feminists are the stewards of their own dreams, movements and communities. We have done this long enough to have a proof of concept for why FRIDA was created in the first place. Young feminist groups need the backing of sustained and trusting resourcing that allows them to grow and organize. 

Giving is political. Every philanthropic decision- who gets funded, who gets scrutinized, and who gets trusted, shapes whose voices are amplified and whose are silenced. In a moment of escalating backlash against gender justice, funding young feminist movements is not a neutral act of generosity or charity. It is an investment in the people defending rights, rebuilding community, and imagining alternatives where none existed before. This Giving Tuesday, give flexibly, give boldly, give to young feminist power.
